author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Denied Education, Denied Choice: The Rise of Child Marriage in Afghanistan
content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, reports of child marriage are increasing. Globally, more than 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year. UN Women identifies education, legal protections, and social support as critical measures for preventing child marriage. Yet in Afghanistan, the Taliban have systematically dismantled these very protections. By banning girls from education beyond the sixth grade, restricting women’s participation in public life, and eliminating pathways to independence, the Taliban are leaving Afghan girls increasingly vulnerable to early and forced marriage.

The Taliban have created an environment in which women and girls are cut off from opportunities, resources, and support systems that would allow them to shape their own futures. With secondary schools and universities closed to girls, millions have lost access to higher education, professional opportunities, and the possibility of financial independence. Restrictions on women’s employment further compound this vulnerability, limiting their ability to support themselves and exercise control over decisions affecting their lives. In addition to these restrictions, the Taliban have issued over 160 decrees and directives affecting all aspects of Afghan girls’ and women’s lives.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Family Caregivers Month: The Economic Burden of Unpaid Care
content:
Every November, National Family Caregivers Month recognizes the millions of Americans who provide care to their loved ones. Caregivers are adult children, spouses, partners, and other loved ones who complete daily tasks and maintain their quality of life. While caregiving is often an expression of love and family responsibility, it also comes with high financial, physical, and emotional costs that frequently go unrecognized.

More than 63 million Americans provide ongoing care for adults or children with complex medical conditions or disabilities. Of these, 59 million care for adults. Around 10% of U.S. adults are caregivers for parents aged 65 or older, while another 3% care for an aging spouse or partner.

The financial burden is particularly pronounced among lower-income households. Among adults with an aging parent, spouse, or partner, 39% of those with lower incomes identify as caregivers, compared with 23% of middle-income adults and 16% of upper-income adults. For caregivers whose household income is less than $40,000, nearly one-third of their income goes toward out-of-pocket expenses related to their loved ones’ needs.

author: Bianca Blell
title: Trump Administration Proposes Cuts to Pregnancy-Related Work Protections
content:
The Trump administration is preparing to narrow federal workplace protections for pregnant workers, potentially limiting access to accommodations for a range of reproductive health conditions.

On November 2nd , the New York Times reported that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) is considering revisions to regulations implementing the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), spearheaded by President Donald Trump. The PWFA was passed by Congress in 2022, initially implemented during the Biden administration.

The original law was meant to fill a gap in disability and discrimination protections that employees are guaranteed in the workplace. Under current regulations, employees are generally required to make reasonable adjustments for qualified employees experiencing pregnancy-related limitations. Examples of such accommodations include additional bathroom breaks, schedule changes, lighter duties, temporary reassignment, and time off for prenatal appointments, including more.

The proposed revisions aim to narrow workplace protections under the PWFA, potentially shrinking the types of accommodations employers are required to provide. author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Unionize After Years of Fighting for Fair Pay
content:
On October 23, 2026, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association was formally and voluntarily recognized as the official collective bargaining representative for the team’s cheer squad. For the first time in the NFL since the Buffalo Jills, an NFL cheer squad successfully unionized, highlighting the need for better protections for cheer team members.

For decades, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders have been among the most recognizable cheerleading squads in professional sports. Despite their prominence and contributions to the team’s brand, members have historically received low wages for demanding work. Before a 400% pay increase for the 2025 season, some veteran cheerleaders reported earning just $15 per hour, in addition to flat fees for games and appearances. Even after the raise, questions about benefits and workplace protections remain.

The pay disparity became particularly visible in 2018, in afederal fair-wage lawsuit filed by Erica Wilkins, a former cheerleader. Wilkins claimed she earned no more than $16,516 in any year of her employment, while the team’s male mascot, Rowdy, earned approximately $65,000 annually. She also alleged that cheerleaders were not compensated for all hours worked, including rehearsals, training, and promotional activities. The lawsuit highlighted the significant pay disparities and lack of labor protections facing women in professional sports.

author: Sofia Little
title: Protests Across the Pond: Gen-Z and the Fight for Affordability in Europe
content:
Across Europe, rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and underfunded public services have fueled a growing wave of protests. Since mid-September, more than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have taken place in 31 European countries. The protests have brought students, workers, and community members into the streets, with young people playing a visible role in organizing and demanding change.

In France, a country with a centuries-long history of protest, the demonstrations began with students demanding more resources for underfunded schools. Students raised concerns about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and crumbling infrastructure. The demonstrations grew into a broader movement, drawing in labor unions and other activists who called out the rising cost of living and declining public services. On October 17th, an estimated 550,000 to 800,00 people protested nationwide.

Other countries began following suit. Since mid-September, demonstrations over high living costs, low wages, and lack of public services have broken out all across Europe. From Spain and Portugal to Germany and Albania, these protests have largely been led by Gen Z. In Spain and Portugal, protesters established encampments in public squares across major cities, demanding stronger laws to protect renters following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

author: Kiara Green
title: Eight Black Women Make History in Georgia Statewide Elections
content:
On November 3, Georgia voters elected eight Black women to statewide office, marking a historic milestone for representation in state government. The victories came as Democratic candidates across the country made significant gains in congressional and state elections, reflecting a shift in the political landscape. Georgia’s results stand out not only for their historic significance, but also for the growing political influence and leadership of Black women across the South.

Over the last decade, Georgia has become increasingly competitive for Democrats, electing Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock to the US Senate. This year, the state elected Keisha Lance Bottom, the former mayor of Atlanta, as governor. Bottoms will become the first Black woman governor and the state’s first Democratic governor elected since 1998.

In her victory speech, Bottoms recognized the broader significance of the results, saying, “And just for the people of Georgia, for us to have had the blue wave, or the blue tsunami, as it’s being described in this state, really represents a shift in Georgia, throughout the South, I believe, that’s going to reshape who we are as a party, as a state for many years to come.”

author: FMF Staff
title: Aisha Wahab’s Victory Shows What Afghan Women Can Achieve. The Taliban Is Denying Afghanistan That Future.
content:
Last week, amid the many historic firsts and important victories in the midterm elections, Afghan American Aisha Wahab won her first full term representing California’s 14th District.

Wahab’s victory is a powerful reminder of what women can accomplish when given the opportunity to lead. Her commitment to public service reflects the talent, determination, and leadership Afghan women bring to their communities and to the world.

At a time when women and girls in Afghanistan are systematically excluded from public life, her achievement is also a reminder of what Afghanistan is losing by denying its women the opportunity to serve, lead, and shape their country’s future.

The contrast could not be more striking.

Wahab’s achievement should not be exceptional. Women’s leadership should be the norm, not the exception. Yet women’s opportunities to lead are still too often denied, obstructed, or dismissed.

Afghan women are just as capable of serving their communities, shaping policy, and holding public office as women anywhere in the world. They have the knowledge, ambition, and commitment. What they need is the opportunity.

author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: Idaho’s OB/GYN Crisis was on the Ballot: Despite Idaho Voting No, the Nation Voted Yes
content:
Following the overturning of Roe, Idaho state law criminalizes abortion at all stages, except in the context of rape or incest that has been formally reported to law enforcement or to prevent the death of the mother. Within fifteen months of the ban’s enactment, 60 OB/GYN physicians stopped practicing obstetrics in Idaho.

As of 2024, 43% of obstetricians have stopped practicing, left the state, closed their practices within the state, or retired in response to harsh legislation. This has left over half of Idaho’s 44 counties without obstetricians, leaving the 23 practicing OB/GYN’s to serve 569,000 Idahoans.

This flight of providers is not a coincidence but rather a clear response to legislation that poses major threats to individuals seeking obstetrician services and physicians. The law’s narrow exceptions and criminal penalties can leave providers concerned about whether an abortion is legally permitted when a patient’s health is at risk. Physicians can be subject to two to five years in prison and risk losing their medical license and being sued for up to $20,000 per family member who chooses to file a lawsuit. This said, the ban’s language is unclear and has left many doctors unsure how to legally interpret the state’s policies and limitations, despite the significant consequences that can follow misinterpretation.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: 2026 Midterms Set New Record for Women Governors, With Historic Firsts Across the Country
content:
The 2026 midterm elections marked a historic breakthrough for women’s representation in state leadership, with voters electing women governors in record numbers and breaking longstanding barriers for women of color. From Georgia to New Mexico, several candidates made history as the first women, Black women, Native American women, and Latina women to lead their states.

In 2027, at least 17 women will serve as governors, representing at least 34% of all governors nationwide. This surpasses the previous record of 14 women governors. This year, 15 women won gubernatorial elections, including 12 Democrats and three Republicans. Two women remain in gubernatorial contests that are too close to call in Alaska and Kansas as of November 5.

Among the most significant victories was Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will become Georgia’s first woman governor and the first Black woman elected governor of any state. The former Atlanta mayor defeated businessman Rick Jackson, ending more than two decades of Republican control of the governor’s office. Bottoms’ victory represents a historic milestone for Black women, who have long been underrepresented in the nation’s highest state offices.

In New Mexico, Deb Haaland will become the first Native American woman governor in US history. A member of the Pueblo of Laguna, Haaland previously served as an US representative and as secretary of the Interior

author: Kiara Green
title: What Rights Are at Stake in the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 Term?
content:
The US Supreme Court reconvened on October 5 for its 2026-27 term which concludes in June of 2027. Cases involving the rights of immigrants, rules governing elections, LGBTQIA rights, and more, stand at the forefront this term. The Court’s decisions could have significant consequences for how federal and state laws protect individual rights.

The Court begins this term with a 6–3 conservative majority. Three of the nine justices, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, were nominated by President Donald Trump. Recent decisions, including the overturning of Dobbs and rulings affecting the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act, have already reshaped the legal landscape. This term, the justices will consider additional disputes over voting regulations and the rights of young people.

Among these cases is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, which is scheduled to be heard on December 8. The Court will decide whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship to register to vote and if the National Voter Registration Act prohibits Arizona from canceling the registrations of non-citizens within 90 days of a federal election.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: A Student’s Guide to Protecting Your Vote on Election Day
content:
As the November 3 midterm elections approach next week, knowing your voting rights and how to respond at the polls is essential to protecting access to the ballot. For students voting on campus or in their local communities, possibly for the first time, it can be particularly confusing when state laws differ or voting procedures are unfamiliar.

Every eligible voter deserves the opportunity to cast a ballot freely, privately, and without intimidation. Here is what voters need to know before heading to the polls.

Federal and state laws protect voters against various forms of discrimination, intimidation and interference. Knowing your rights can help you recognize when to ask for assistance.

You have the right to equal treatment. Federal law prohibits discrimination in voting on protected grounds, including race and color. Other federal and state laws, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act, provide additional protections related to accessible polling places and language assistance. Voters who need assistance due to disability or difficulty reading/writing English have the right to bring a person of their choice into the voting booth to assist them, as long as that person is not their employer or union representative.

author: FMF Staff
title: Deporting Afghans to the Taliban by Way of Pakistan Is a Betrayal That Gets the United States Nothing
content:
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing to put more than 150 Afghans on a flight to Pakistan, where they would then be transferred across the border into Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. AfghanEvac, a coalition advocating for Afghan allies, says some of those facing removal are the brothers and sons of men who served alongside U.S. forces. The first flight could leave as early as Monday, just one day before Election Day in the United States.

Because the United States cannot deport people directly to Afghanistan, it lacks official diplomatic relations with the Taliban regime; the plan routes them through Pakistan. Call it what it is: a deportation to the Taliban with a layover. Officials reportedly told The New York Times that the removal is, in effect, to Afghanistan, and detainees have been told the same. Pakistan’s role is to carry out the handoff.

What the layover adds is risk. Afghans would be moved through a third country and beyond any oversight, and placed in the hands of authorities who have no obligation to protect them. From there, they could be pushed across the border to a regime they fled and one that would seek to harm them. These are the people who escaped Taliban rule after August 15, 2021.

author: Madelyn Amos
title: ¡Sí Se Puede!: Dolores Huerta’s Feminist Legacy Lives On
content:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader, civil rights activist, and feminist who devoted her life to advancing equality and justice, has died at the age of 96. Her groundbreaking work reshaped the labor and feminist movements, leaving an enduring legacy of grassroots organizing, women’s leadership, and collective action that continues to inspire generations.

Huerta was a dear friend and ally of the Feminist Majority Foundation since its founding. She served on the organization’s board for more than 30 years, offering her passion, energy, and visionary leadership to the fight for gender equality.

In the 1980s, Feminist Majority co-founders Eleanor Smeal and Kathy Spillar recruited Huerta to join the Feminization of Power campaign to increase women’s representation in elected office. For four years, Huerta traveled across the country with the Feminist Majority. She mentored women running for office, particularly Latinas and other women of color, and helped them secure endorsements while campaigning alongside them.

Reflecting on their work together, Smeal recalled, “We traveled to 8 states and she was determined to change the composition of California’s state legislature — and she did.
